title: Why time speeds up as we age
text: Almost everyone notices that time {{1}} up as we get older: childhood summers stretched without end, while a recent year can pass in what feels like weeks. The {{2}} explanation is mathematical. To a ten-year-old, a year is a tenth of everything remembered; to a fifty-year-old, a fiftieth — so each new year is, proportionally, briefer. But arithmetic {{3}} only half the story, because the {{4}} half lies in memory rather than ratios. Brains {{5}} space by refusing to store the routine: identical commutes and familiar weeks are compressed to almost nothing, while first experiences get the full treatment. Measured in remembered {{6}}, a single novel week abroad can outlast a whole grey season at home. This also explains the cure, and the {{7}} are pleasantly undemanding: take unfamiliar routes, learn awkward new skills, rearrange the furniture of your routines. Novelty forces the brain to record in detail, and detail is what makes a period feel long afterwards. The clock, in other words, ticks at the {{8}} speed for everyone; it is memory that decides how much of life you actually get to keep.

gaps.explanation: 'time speeds up' — phrasal verb for going faster.
'the obvious explanation is mathematical' — the one everyone notices; the arithmetic account is not awkward, suspicious or random.
'arithmetic tells only half the story' — fixed expression.
'the other half' — the second of two known halves.
'brains save space by not storing routine' — economise.
'measured in remembered time' — uncountable duration; dates, calendars and clocks are counting devices, not the substance itself.
'the implications are pleasantly undemanding' — the practical consequences; the listed tips follow from the theory, and complications, symptoms and reactions clash with 'pleasantly'.
'ticks at the same speed' — fixed: the same, not 'a steady'.
